Your perception surprises you

The Ponzo illusion and the railway tracks

Two equal lines between converging lines look different in size. The brain applies perspective even when it is not needed.

In 1911, the Italian psychologist Mario Ponzo described a very simple illusion. Draw two lines that come together towards the top, like railway tracks disappearing into the distance. Place two identical horizontal lines between them, one high and one low. The upper one looks longer.

Automatic perspective

The most accepted explanation is that the brain reads converging lines as a cue to depth. The upper line seems farther away and, since it takes up the same space on the retina, the brain concludes it must actually be larger.

It is the same correction that lets us see a distant person as normal-sized rather than as a tiny doll. The illusion shows that this correction is automatic: even when we know the lines are equal, we keep seeing them as different.

References

  1. Ponzo, M. (1911). Intorno ad alcune illusioni nel campo delle sensazioni tattili, sull'illusione di Aristotele e fenomeni analoghi. Archiv für die gesamte Psychologie, 16, 307–345.
  2. Gregory, R. L. (1997). Eye and Brain (5.ª ed.). Princeton University Press.
